content: Chemical equilibrium occurs when the rates of forward and reverse reactions become equal, resulting in no net change in reactant and product concentrations over time. Unlike static equilibrium, this is a dynamic state where reactions continue in both directions at the same rate. Le Chatelier's Principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the system will shift to counteract the change and establish a new equilibrium. Increasing reactant concentration shifts equilibrium toward products; decreasing it shifts toward reactants. Temperature changes affect equilibrium position based on reaction enthalpyâendothermic reactions favor products when temperature increases, while exothermic reactions favor reactants. Pressure changes affect equilibrium in gas-phase reactions by shifting toward the side with fewer gas molecules when pressure increases. The equilibrium constant (Kâq) expresses the relationship between product and reactant concentrations at equilibrium: Kâq = [products]/[reactants]. A large Kâq (>1) indicates equilibrium favors products; a small Kâq (<1) means reactants are favored. Catalysts speed up both forward and reverse reactions equally, helping a system reach equilibrium faster without changing the equilibrium position.

scenario.title: Cafeteria Equilibrium
scenario.content: Students manage a virtual school cafeteria where they control factors affecting the flow of students entering and leaving. The simulation represents chemical species as different student types, with entrance and exit rates analogous to reaction rates. Students can adjust 'concentration' (number of waiting students), 'temperature' (serving speed), 'pressure' (cafeteria capacity), and 'catalysts' (additional serving stations) to observe how these changes affect the system's equilibrium. Real-time graphs show rate changes and concentration profiles as the system responds to disturbances. The simulation visually demonstrates Le Chatelier's Principle as the system adjusts to reach new equilibrium states after interventions. Advanced features allow students to calculate equilibrium constants and predict how specific changes will affect system behavior.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze chemical equilibrium systems by examining how reaction rates balance at the molecular level. They will predict how changes in concentration, temperature, pressure, and catalysts affect equilibrium position, and apply Le Chatelier's Principle to explain system responses to disturbances.
